text: Retivo architecture overview. How the pieces fit together.
Local-first.
The working copy of your plan is kept in the browser, in IndexedDB.
Every projection, tax estimate, and Monte Carlo run happens right there, with the heavy runs in web workers.
The server never computes anything about your plan. If it's unreachable, the app keeps working.
The components.
The web app is React. It owns the storage, the sync client, the encryption, and the calculation engine.
The API is NestJS, plus the entry points of the background Lambdas.
Contracts holds the shared Zod schemas. Infrastructure is a Pulumi program that builds the A-W-S resources.
Local versus A-W-S.
Locally, the API is a plain Node process. DynamoDB Local and Moto stand in for the database, storage, and email.
The emulators keep their data in memory, so a restart wipes it. Local runs are for development and testing only.
Deployed, CloudFront serves the web app from S3, and forwards slash API to API Gateway and a Lambda, backed by DynamoDB and S3.
The API code is the same. Settings point it at emulators or to A-W-S. For UI work, a mock transport removes the server entirely.
Signing in.
The API checks your password against an Argon2id hash, and returns a five-minute access token, kept in memory only.
A refresh token is kept in an HttpOnly cookie, and rotates on every use. Deployed stacks also require a second factor.
Then comes unlocking. The household key is stored on the server only in wrapped form, in slots: password, recovery key, and optionally a passkey.
Any one slot opens it, in the browser. The server never sees the key.
Sync.
An edit is saved to IndexedDB first, so the screen reacts at once, and queued as a mutation.
The sync client encrypts the payload, and pushes the batch.
The server checks each record's version, refuses plaintext, and stores only ciphertext.
Other devices pull the changes after a cursor. A new device bootstraps from the latest snapshot.
When changes collide.
If the version the browser saw is stale, the server rejects that change as a conflict.
Auto-repair drops duplicates, or re-applies the change on the server's version. Anything else shows in the sync badge, for you to decide.
A row that won't decrypt is quarantined on that device, and the rest still loads. A freshness counter catches a server serving older data.
Snapshots.
The compactor Lambda writes an encrypted snapshot to S3, then trims the part of the mutation log it covers.
It only deletes what the snapshot provably contains. A device whose cursor has expired bootstraps again.
The janitor deletes old snapshots daily, and you can restore your household to any snapshot that's kept.
What the server can see.
Your account details, and for each change, the record id, type, version, time, and size.
It cannot read the contents of a plan.
One caveat: data on your device isn't encrypted at rest, so protect the device itself.
That's the architecture. Local first, end-to-end encrypted, and synced through a server that can't read your plan.
